Flier (Centrarchus macropterus) is a small centrarchid endemic to the Atlantic and Gulf slope drainages of the southeastern United States, where it inhabits swampy, slow-moving waters. Field surveys in coastal plain streams indicate that newly hatched individuals emerge from demersal adhesive eggs at a remarkably small size, with wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.0045 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0045 grams]. This minimal initial mass, roughly equivalent to a single fraction of a gram, reflects the tiny yolk stores available to the prolarva upon eclosion. The developing yolk-sac larva undergoes a rapid endogenous feeding phase before yolk absorption completion, after which the exotrophic transition must occur within a narrow window to avoid starvation. During the pelagic larval phase, growth is heavily temperature-dependent, and metabolic demands escalate quickly as the free-swimming larva begins active prey capture in the plankton-rich backwater habitats that characterize typical flier nursery grounds across the region.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under laboratory conditions approximating the thermal regime of its natural environment. At a stable water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate is derived from observations of captive spawning pairs that each produce approximately 103 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 103 eggs per spawning event] with an estimated frequency of roughly 365 such events per year [F_R_i = roughly 365 such events per year]. This relatively modest fecundity per event, when compared to other centrarchids of similar body size, suggests a spawning strategy that emphasizes repeated small clutches rather than a single massive pulse of gametes. The gravid females deposit their clutches in shallow depressions they excavate in soft substrate, and males guard the developing embryos until chorion rupture, a period lasting roughly a week. Such extended parental investment likely offsets the vulnerability of the pelagic egg stage and increases the probability of larval recruitment into the juvenile population in these hydrologically variable habitats across the southeastern coastal plain.

Sexual maturation in Flier proceeds along a trajectory that can be inferred from length-at-age data collected from archived museum series across the species' range. The total length at puberty is approximately 7.0 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7.0 centimeters], a size that individuals typically attain around three years after hatching [tp = around three years after hatching], based on annuli counts from sagittal otoliths. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is calculated at 6.2 grams [Wwp = 6.2 grams], derived from length-weight regressions specific to this species. This relatively extended maturation period, compared to more rapidly maturing congeners such as Lepomis macrochirus, likely reflects the energy-limited conditions in dystrophic swamp environments where food resources can be variable. The onset of gametogenesis appears cued by a combination of increasing photoperiod and rising spring water temperatures, leading to the first spawning event for most individuals in their fourth calendar year. This reproductive schedule positions the species as a moderately late-maturing iteroparous centrarchid.

Body size at adulthood in Flier is modest relative to other members of the family Centrarchidae. The ultimate total length is 35.6 centimeters [Li = 35.6 centimeters], representing the maximum standard length recorded across multiple populations, and the corresponding ultimate wet weight is 954 grams [Wwi = 954 grams], established from the species-specific length-mass allometry. This asymptotic mass is considerably less than that of largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) or other large centrarchids, a disparity that reflects the flier's evolutionary adaptation to nutrient-poor, acidic blackwater habitats where maximum body size is constrained. Adult individuals exhibit a deep, laterally compressed body form that facilitates maneuverability within densely vegetated margins of cypress swamps and sluggish bayous. Diet studies indicate that mature fliers feed primarily on benthic macroinvertebrates, with occasional piscivory when prey fish are abundant. This moderate maximum size likely contributes to the species' ecological niche partitioning within diverse centrarchid assemblages across the region.

Longevity records for Flier indicate a relatively extended lifespan for a centrarchid of its body size, particularly given the energetic demands of its reproductive strategy. The maximum time since birth at death has been documented at 8 years [am = 8 years] under natural conditions at a water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], with the oldest individuals typically originating from populations in stable, predator-limited coastal plain refugia. This lifespan, which translates to approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days] at the same thermal regime, suggests that senescence-related mortality is gradual rather than catastrophic in this species at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. Growth models fitted to mark-recapture data indicate that individuals continue to increase in both length and body mass well into their sixth year, with asymptotic size approached only late in life. Comparative studies across the genus Centrarchus reveal that fliers are among the longer-lived members of their clade, a trait that may be linked to their relatively low metabolic rate in cool, oxygen-poor swamp habitats. Field observations of tagged individuals confirm that reproductive output remains substantial even in older age classes, supporting an iteroparous life-history strategy.
